chapters.title: One Room in the Whole World
The Well That Learned to Say No

lines.text: Everything in this harbour is made up, except the kind of room in that window.
It is a chat room, the very example Durable Objects began with, in 2020.
Someone types message forty-two: the ferry is late.
It waits at the door. Then it gets its tick: a promise that it is saved.
Then House A goes dark, and the square goes quiet.
Up the hill, House C lights. Its keeper, the runtime, draws a bundle from the well, and the room relights in a new window.
Message forty-two is still there, with its tick.
The machine that made that promise is gone. The promise is still true.
How did the promise outlive the machine?
The answer is in the square: the town well, which is a storage bucket.
The plate above it names the room's owner.
The room keeps two promises: one owner at a time, and nothing acknowledged is lost when a machine fails.
And a newer one, still being built: the room can move between machines you run.
So how can a bucket, which cannot run a single line of code, make a room portable?
A story from 2020 to the end of October 2026: a room, a well and a ribbon.
The harbour is ours. The machinery is real code, and every piece wears a tag saying whose.
The newest of it is days old, and still experimental.
On the twenty-eighth of September, 2020, Kenton Varda of Cloudflare introduced Durable Objects, in a closed beta.
Each object has an identifier that is unique across the whole world.
And his post is plain about where that object lives.
In one place. Only ever one, at a time.
So every request about the same thing reaches the same place, and that place can coordinate them.
His demonstration is a chat app: each chat room is one object, and every message passes through it to everyone else.
That is the kind of room our lantern holds: one room, one object, one home.
Notice what one home does not mean. A handler can stop and wait, and living in one place does not make all its steps one transaction.
The third of August, 2021. A later post of his is called Easy, Fast, Correct: Choose three.
It puts a gate on the room's door, an output gate. While a write is unfinished, the reply to our sender waits behind a latch.
The write completes. The latch lifts, and the letter goes out.
If the write fails, the waiting letters are thrown away, replaced with errors, and the object restarts.
So the tick in the harbour was a held letter, released.
September 2022. Cloudflare opens the source of its runtime, workerd.
Now the runtime could leave Cloudflare, and a room could come too, but only as a single instance on one machine. In 2026 Ryan Dahl would call it exactly that: limited to a single instance.
September 2024. SQLite moves inside the object, into the very same thread as its code.
Local reads become almost instant.
But a tick is not a local read. A tick says the write will outlive the machine.
On Cloudflare's own network, a hosted service kept that promise: the Storage Relay Service.
It watches SQLite's write-ahead log, where each change is written first, and ships the changes to object storage in batches: ten seconds, or sixteen megabytes, at the most.
Object storage is slow, and nobody can wait ten seconds for a tick.
So each commit also goes straight to five followers, in five different data centres. When three answer, the latch lifts.
Real machinery. And all of it lived inside Cloudflare.
Back to the square. In our harbour the Well stands for a bucket in an object store, like Amazon's S3.
There was a time when overwriting a file in S3 and reading it straight back could hand you the old copy.
Amazon later explained why: a write could take one path through its caches, and a read another.
On the first of December, 2020, that changed: read after a write, and you get the latest.
Whatever bucket you draw up is the newest.
The job: the room's Plate is empty, and Houses A and B both want it.
Fresh reads are not enough. Pull the pin from the Well's brass tooth, and the Well checks nothing.
Each keeper reads the Plate: nobody. Each writes: mine.
Both lanterns light; both rooms take messages.
B's plate lands a moment later and wins the Well. But A has already answered its senders.
An overwrite can win the well. It cannot take back what was already served.
Between the read and the write, the world moved. Pin back.
The twentieth of August, 2024. S3 learns its first refusal: write this only if nothing is there.
Two keepers race. One creation lands, a shutter drops, and the second card is refused.
The twenty-fifth of November, 2024: replace this only if it is still the version I read.
Both cards carry the same old version. One click: accepted, and the Plate's notch is cut anew. One thunk: refused.
That is compare and swap, and the store checks the condition, not the keeper.
The Well had learned to say no.
So who referees the referee?
In April 2021, Werner Vogels, Amazon's chief technology officer, described what they had built inside S3.
Caches that agree with one another, an order for every object's changes, and a witness, told of every change, that any cache can ask: is my copy stale?
They checked it with proofs and model checking, which, he wrote, was more work than building it.
So the houses on the hill run no consensus of their own. The coordination has moved inside the Well.
Now a warning, from celld's own documentation.
Some stores speak S3's language but do not keep these conditions; on them, two houses can own one room.
Worse, a store can accept the condition and silently ignore it.
So before it serves, every celld node makes four test writes: create, refuse a second create, update, refuse a stale update. Two must fail.
Then it checks a ranged read. No node can skip the test.
A bucket earns its place by refusing, on demand.
One more thing to notice. The Well referees one key at a time: one Plate for one room.
It makes no promise that two rooms commit as one.
And if the Well goes quiet, no house can take a Plate at all.
August, 2026. A second desk, a second lamp: the Deno team releases celld.
Ryan Dahl, of Deno, had started it, and he later told us why.
He wanted a single binary, written in Rust, whose only outside service is object storage.
celld runs a Workers application on machines you own: Durable Objects, self-hosted and distributed, with long-term state in a bucket.
Its README says it needs no consensus service. By now we know where the consensus went: inside the well.
Its log replicator descends from a Rust reimplementation of Litestream.
In October the two would write one post together. In it, Kenton Varda, of Cloudflare, named the gap.
workerd's Durable Objects ran as a single instance: good enough for local testing, unable to scale. He called it workerd's one big gap in production readiness.
And he wrote that when the Deno team released celld in August, “we were delighted.”
Two lamps in one frame. Two ropes, beginning to braid.
On the ninth of October, 2026, Deno and Cloudflare announced that the whole Deno team was joining Cloudflare.
These are plans, as announced. The Deno runtime gets one more year of bug-fix and security releases.
After that year, Ryan Dahl writes, the team's work on the Deno runtime comes to an end.
Deno Deploy runs six more months. JSR and rusty_v8 continue. Deno stays open source.
Cloudflare filed its post under acquisitions, yet neither post states a price or any terms. We will not guess at them.
Ryan Dahl and Bert Belder are to lead a first-class, supported way to run workerd yourself.
On the evening of the twenty-eighth of October, Pacific time, Ryan Dahl's commit landed in workerd, calling itself a beginning.
Several processes share one bucket; each object has one owner at a time, and if an owner dies, the message says, another picks it up.
It is experimental. For now, a write is acknowledged only once the bucket holds all of it.
And one plain line: “Alarms are not supported yet.”
Two days later, alarms landed. The next day, facets.
Let us open it.
Open the Plate. In workerd's cluster it has three tiles: the house that owns the room, an epoch, and a third, called from.
The epoch is a count that goes up with every new claim. The from tile names the last epoch that actually opened.
The code calls it the only authority on who owns the room.
To claim, a keeper offers the version it read. If the Plate names a house whose lease has run out, the claim writes the next epoch, and at most one claimant wins.
If that house is still alive, the request goes there instead. A brand-new room is born already open.

terms.gloss: the middle tile of the Plate

lines.text: A house may serve only while it holds a lease: a candle on its sill, relit at each renewal.
In workerd the lease is twenty seconds. A house renews every three, gives each attempt four, and retries a failure after one.
A clock may be two seconds off the bucket's, so the painted band at the candle's foot is twice that: four seconds.
If this lease runs out at twenty thousand milliseconds, the house may serve only while its clock reads under sixteen thousand.
And it may start a renewal only under twelve thousand, so even a full four-second attempt ends before the band.
Lines on a ruler, not promises about timers.
Why give each renewal four seconds, and not two? The code keeps a scar.
A comment records that Cloudflare's R2 stalls writes for about five and a half seconds at every five-minute mark, and that a two-second limit once stopped every node.
So failed renewals are retried while the lease still holds through the attempt.
A's keeper falls asleep: a paused process.
Pull the pin, so A never checks its own candle.
The candle burns through the band. B sees that A's lease has run out, and claims the room.
A wakes and goes on serving. Two rooms.
Pin back. Waking, A checks its candle first. Past the band, it serves nothing, closes its own shutters, and its lamp goes out.
A house that cannot renew in time does the same while its lease still holds: gone before anyone may take over. That is fencing.
Notice what B never knew. A timeout proves silence. It does not prove death.
Safety comes from A stopping itself, and from a second look at the Plate.
One soft spot: each house measures its clock against the bucket's, and when it cannot, it assumes zero.
So the clock is not the last line of defence; the second look is.
celld, a different implementation, uses ten-second leases, and when the Well proves a write it does the same: it reads the record, not a clock.
Claimed is not opened, and the difference decides which past the room comes back with.
Made-up numbers. A opened epoch seven: A, seven, from seven. The crown is lit.
B claims: B, eight, from seven. The from tile stays at seven, and the crown is dark.
To open, B must restore seven's log, upload a snapshot, and then make the opening write that sets the from tile to eight.
That flicker in House B, the night A went dark? B died first. C claims: C, nine, from seven, and recovers seven, because eight never opened and acknowledged nothing.
Rewind. Had B opened, the Plate would read B, eight, from eight, and C would recover eight.
Inside the lantern, SQLite keeps the room in a file. But it does not write changes there first.
It writes them to a second file beside it: a write-ahead log. Think of it as a ribbon.
It starts with a leader, thirty-two bytes long. Then frames: each a twenty-four-byte tab and one page.
On a transaction's last frame, the tab records how many pages the database has after the commit. Other frames hold zero there.
We draw it as a red stamp. That number is the commit mark.
workerd's keeper hears every write to the ribbon, holds the frames since the last stamp, and cuts only when a stamped frame is complete.
One cut, one whole transaction. Nothing half-finished ever leaves the room.
A transaction that rolls back leaves frames with no stamp, and the next writes straight over them.
When SQLite copies the ribbon into its main file and starts a fresh one, the keeper starts fresh too.
The cut lengths go down to the Well as scrolls: each page once, in its newest version.
Every scroll's cord records a checksum and its length, so a damaged or short scroll refuses to be read, rather than read wrong.
Each epoch's shelf starts with a Book, a snapshot of what it inherited; a new Book goes down before old scrolls are cleared.
This is workerd's own format. celld writes a different one, called LTX.
Now the tick itself, in workerd. Message forty-two is written; its reply waits behind the latch.
The keeper cuts the transaction, and sends the scroll down to the Well.
Then, before it rings the bell, the keeper looks up at the Plate one more time. Still A. Still epoch seven.
Only then the bell. The latch lifts. The tick.
Finishing inside the room is not the tick. The Well and the second look are. celld's gate holds even more: errors, and every chunk of a stream.
Pull the pin, and the keeper never looks up.
A sends its scroll with its lease in order, then the whole house freezes, like the sleeper. B claims epoch eight, and A's scroll lands on epoch seven's shelf.
A rings the bell anyway: a tick for a write that B may never see.
Pin back. A looks up: the Plate says eight. No bell; the letter becomes an error, and the old scroll is cleared later.
One honest limit: if a reply is lost on its way home, the sender cannot tell whether the write happened.
A missing tick does not prove a write absent. Durability is not the same as exactly once.
Back to workerd's town, the night A went dark. House C holds the Plate: nine, from seven.
First it throws away its own copy of the room.
It reads the newest Book, then each scroll in order, skipping pages already laid down.
A missing scroll in the middle stops the restore cold.
A checksum can say a scroll is damaged. Never what it said.
Pages are laid down again; no code is re-run.
Message forty-two is back. Only then does C send down its own Book, and open the Plate.
That is the price. In workerd's cluster, every tick waits for the Well, and a second look at the Plate.
Our bar is illustrative: a sliver of local work, then the long walk.
Cloudflare's hosted relay, back in 2024, answered that with followers.
celld uses followers too: a neighbour's disk can answer much sooner than the Well.
Change the lamps.
This is celld's town, version 0.6.3. By default, the owner hands each write to one or two neighbours.
Each must press the page onto its own disk before it answers. That press is called fsync.
When every neighbour in the proof has pressed, the bell can ring before the page reaches the Well. The upload follows.
Now count. The owner never counts itself.
One house alone gets no fleet. It falls back on the Well's proof: much slower, still correct.
Two running houses: one neighbour, enough for a proof. Three or more: two neighbours, three copies.
Until a second neighbour joins, a fresh write's proof rests on two copies: the owner's and one neighbour's.
Now replay that night in celld's town: the owner dies while forty-two lives only in the neighbours' notebooks.
Pull the pin.
In celld's Well, each epoch writes under its own shelf, so a stale owner can only add to an old shelf, never to the new owner's.
That fences the Well. It cannot fetch what only the neighbours hold. Forty-two is gone.
Or the old owner was only asleep, and wakes to ring one more bell.
Pin back. Before its first tick from the neighbours, each celld session creates its own log record in the Well.
So a successor reads that record before it reads the Well.
Absent: the old session never ticked ahead of the Well. Sealed: someone already recovered it.
Open, or still recovering: fence it with a compare and swap. Seal every neighbour it can reach, collect their pages, upload them, and mark the record sealed.
Only then restore. With its neighbours sealed, the old owner cannot win another bell.
Now the hard rule. At least one current neighbour must hand over its complete range of retained pages.
Two made-up cases. One notebook is water-damaged, but the other is complete: recovery proceeds.
Now one notebook is incomplete, and the other damaged. Nobody can prove the whole tail, so the door stays shut.
And a neighbour that answers with an error has not proved its pages absent.
The room would rather stay shut than come back missing a promise.
Houses that restart together still lend each other their notebooks. Recovery can take minutes; a waiting request gives up only after two hundred and forty tries.
In our harbour the notebooks are whole. The lantern relights; forty-two keeps its tick.
Four pins, in the order we pulled them: the Tooth, the band on the candle, the second look, the neighbours' seal.
Pull any one, and a promise breaks.
So what travels, when a room travels, is not the bucket alone.
It is the bucket's refusals on one key, and its fresh reads; leases, with clocks kept close; and, as celld asks, a supervisor to restart a house that fenced itself.
And a runtime that cuts the ribbon, uploads and looks again; in celld's fleet, one that also seals and collects before it replays.
The small print, as of the thirty-first of October, 2026.
workerd's clustering is three days old, and still experimental.
Its tests check one writer, forwarding, and takeover after a kill. We read them. We did not run them.
The alarm tests check the cases they stage. They do not establish exactly-once effects for every application.
celld documents its own limits, and wants bucket lifecycle rules that leave its records alone.
And workerd, on its own, is not a sandbox for untrusted code.
The two lamps, once more. The announced plan stands, and the commit called itself a beginning.
celld's code and ideas are to be merged into workerd, and Ryan Dahl writes that the team's future work goes into this shared platform.
And the Well? It does not run your code, make two rooms commit as one, promise exactly once, or keep the town open when it goes quiet.
Dawn over the harbour. The lantern burns in House C, and the sender's slip still carries its tick.
A tick is not a feeling. It is a proof.
The bytes were in the Well, and the Plate still named its owner when the bell rang.
The harbour was made up. The code is real.
